chapter_theme: The decade of the other woman's sulking (புலவி விராய பத்து, marutham, Orampokiyar): the courtesan answers the husband, the bard and her own friend about the wife's anger, mocking the husband's straying, the wife's jealousy and the title of wife, and ending with the husband as a bee (81-90).

81.reading: The other woman tells the lord of the town, where field workers with their rattling drum add to their evening meal the white-bellied turtle a heron has cracked open, by a pond whose mouth is decked with flowers, that if his wife heard him say 'I desired you' to her, she would grieve greatly.
81.nuance: Her concern for the wife is mock concern: she turns his declaration of love back on him as something he could not say at home, so the line that seems kind is a taunt. The heron that cracks the turtle and the workers who gather what is left can be read as the man who takes his pleasure and the women who live on his leavings, but the poem names no second match and draws no moral, so it fails condition 3 and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: field workers, a pond turtle and a flowered pond are things of the watered fields

82.reading: The other woman tells the bard that, they say, his mistress flew into a rage because the bees that fed on the pollen of the fragrant garland of open clusters on her husband's chest came and settled in her own flower-filled hair.
82.nuance: The proof against him is so slight that it is comic: a few bees moving from his garland to her hair. She lets the bard carry back that the wife's anger is out of proportion, while admitting the closeness the bees reveal. The bees are not iraicchi: strike them and the wife's anger has no cause, so they are the poem's subject (the deletion test fails).

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's anger at a husband who has been with another woman is marutham's sulking

83.reading: The other woman tells the man who joined with her and now shows no grace that he should at least draw away gently and let her survive, so that even the bright-bangled girls of his town may say of the lord of the cool ford that he was hers once.
83.nuance: She does not ask him to stay, only to leave slowly, so that the break looks like a fading and not a dismissal; what she guards is how she will be spoken of among the town's girls, her standing rather than his love.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the cool ford is the marutham man

84.reading: The other woman says that the wife, who rages beyond words when she only hears of it, what will she become when she sees with her own eyes his philandering chest, which many plunge into and enjoy like the cool pond of the month of Thai where women with fragrant flowers in their braids bathe.
84.nuance: She includes herself among the many who bathe in that pond, so the simile is a boast as well as a charge: the chest is common, and she has had her share. The Thai bath was a girls' vow for a good husband, which makes the pond an ironic image for a husband shared by all.

thinai_evidence.note: the bathing pond of the Thai festival is the field country's water

85.reading: The other woman tells the lord of the town of flawless, overflowing new wealth, where the white-browed water-hen's rattling-voiced mate calls among her kin in the cool fragrant field-pond, that he does things like a little boy: won't those who see him laugh?
85.nuance: The address swings from the grand (பெரும, lord of rich new wealth) to the belittling (like little boys), and the mockery lives in that gap. The hen calling among her kin could be read as a woman secure in her household, but it does nothing a person of the situation does, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-hen of the field-pond is a marutham bird

86.reading: The other woman tells the lord of the town, where the soft-winged white-headed heron's calling voice echoes across the long fields, that it is hard for him to grace her here, so let him go and join the young woman of his house.
86.nuance: Sending him home is her sulk: she calls the wife a மடந்தை, a young girl, which both concedes the wife's claim and belittles it.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron calling over long paddy fields fixes the field country

87.reading: The other woman tells the lord of the rich town, where cowherds of many cattle, wearing pakanrai chaplets, knock down mangoes using sugarcane as a stick, that his wife sulks at everyone, so why single her out?
87.nuance: A town so rich that herdsmen use sugarcane to beat down mangoes is a town of careless plenty, and the wife who sulks at all comers is pictured as just as indiscriminate; a reader may see the cane-stick as the wife's anger spent on anyone, but only one match can be named, so it is a near miss on condition 3 and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: sugarcane, mango and a rich town are marutham plenty; the cowherds are guests from the pasture

88.reading: The other woman says that they report our sister, his wife, wanting the lord of the cool ford of the rich flowered pond where the bees dwell to come to her; she too, as if she were one of his old ones, wants just that.
88.nuance: Calling the wife எவ்வை, our sister, places the two women in one family of his women; the claim to want him 'like old ones' (தொல்லேம் போல்) mocks the wife's claim of seniority by borrowing it.

thinai_evidence.note: a bee-haunted flower pond at a cool ford is the field country

89.reading: The other woman tells the bard that people ask what great grace the lord of the town, where bees sip pollen in the field-pond, shows our sister: it is her own nature that wished to be called his wife.
89.nuance: The barb is that the wife has the name of wife (பெண்டு) and is content with it; the grace she is said to receive is her title, not his love. The bee sipping pollen in the epithet foreshadows the bee image of poem 90 but does nothing a person does here beyond the epithet, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: bees in the field-pond fix the field country

90.reading: The other woman wonders whether the bees took on the husband's fine nature or the husband took on the bees', and says that the mother of his son, not knowing he is so, sulks with her.
90.nuance: The 'fine quality' (மாண்குணம்) shared by bee and husband is flitting from flower to flower, so the praise is the sharpest insult in the decade; and the wife is named only as the mother of his son, the one bond the other woman cannot share.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulk at the husband's other woman is marutham's situation

links.note: Ainkurunuru 81: the other woman says his wife would grieve if she heard him say he desired her. Natrinai 100: the other woman laughs at how the man trembled when she said she would go and tell his wife.
links.teaches: In both the other woman's hold on the man is the wife's knowledge: the Ainkurunuru voices it as mock pity for the wife, the Natrinai as a threat that sets him shaking, so together they show that the courtesan's power in marutham rests on what the wife may hear.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman calls his chest a Thai bathing pond that many plunge into. Kural 1311: the wife refuses his chest because all women feast on it with their eyes.
links.teaches: The Kural wife's complaint that his chest is common property is made, in the Ainkurunuru, by one of the women who share it, who boasts of it rather than complains, so the same image of the common chest serves as reproach from the house and as triumph from outside it.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common field-pond (பழனம்). Ainkurunuru 84: the other woman says his chest is a pond where many bathe.
links.teaches: The decade of wishes prays against exactly the outcome this decade reports, his chest as a pond for all, so the anthology's own order sets the bride's fear and the courtesan's taunt in one image eight decades apart.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 87: the other woman says the wife sulks at everyone, so why at her. Akananuru 186: the courtesan says the wife quarrels with her (எம்மொடு புலக்கும்), but she is not the enemy; the husband who leaves women pale is.
links.teaches: The four-line protest that the wife's sulk is aimless becomes in the Akananuru a full defence that redirects the blame to the husband, so the pair shows the courtesan's answer to the wife's anger as a set speech with two steps: she is not singled out, and the fault lives in the wife's own house.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 89: the other woman tells the bard the wife is greatly graced, only because she wants the name of wife. Naladiyar 390: the wife tells the bard not to lie that he will be kind; she is the dry end of the cane and the others its sweet middle. On a plain reading each woman says the other has his favour.
links.teaches: Each woman tells the same messenger that the other is the favoured one, so the bard meets the identical complaint at both doors and the triangle has no one who admits to being loved; the Naladiyar files that voice under the chaste wife, the Ainkurunuru gives it to the rival.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 90: the other woman says the husband has the bee's nature, and his son's mother wrongly sulks with her. Kuruntokai 8: the other woman says the man boasts in her house but at home moves like a mirror image to whatever his son's mother wants.
links.teaches: Both courtesans name the wife only as his son's mother, but one says he roves like a bee and the other that he obeys his wife like a puppet, so together they show the other woman claiming no hold on him at all: he belongs to every flower and, at home, to the mother of his son.

source_issues: 81-90: the colophon has no thurai for this decade; the speaker (parathai) and addressees are inferred from the poems and the decade title புலவி விராய பத்து, so occasion words are null.
81 line 1: உடைத் தூண்ட is printed split; read as உடைத்து உண்ட.
88 line 4 and 89 lines 2 and 4: the e-text joins and splits words (வேண் டுதுமே, பெரி தளிக்கும்) so the exact sense of the wish and of பெண்டென விரும்பின்று is uncertain.
